title: Freelance Project Wrap-Up Kit
description: Finish every project so it pays you twice: a six-stage wrap-up checklist, a client handover document with a completed example, eight closing and check-in emails, a seven-question feedback form, a case study template and a follow-up tracker for repeat work and referrals.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Project Wrap-Up Kit

The end of a project is where most freelancers lose money they have already earned: the final invoice goes out late, files get handed over in a mess, nobody asks for feedback, and a happy client quietly forgets you exist. This kit turns the last week of every project into a short routine that gets you paid, leaves the client impressed, and brings back repeat work and referrals.

It is built for solo freelancers and small studios doing project work: design, writing, development, marketing, video, photography, consulting and similar.

## What's inside

| File | Use it for |
|---|---|
| wrap-up-checklist.md | The full routine from "final draft approved" to "project archived", in five stages. |
| handover-document-template.md | A one-page handover the client keeps: what they got, where it lives, how to use it. Includes a completed example. |
| closing-emails.md | Eight ready-to-send emails: final delivery, final invoice, feedback request, review permission, referral ask, and three check-ins at 1, 3 and 6 months. |
| feedback-questions.md | A short client feedback form (seven questions) plus how to read the answers and what to change. |
| case-study-template.md | Turn a finished project into a portfolio case study in 45 minutes. Includes a completed example. |
| client-follow-up-tracker.csv | One row per finished project: dates of each follow-up, feedback score, permission to quote, referrals and repeat work. Opens in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers. |

## Quick start (20 minutes, once)

1. Read **wrap-up-checklist.md** from top to bottom so you know the shape of the routine.
2. Put your name, business name and sign-off into the brackets in **closing-emails.md** and save your own copy.
3. Save **handover-document-template.md** as your own document with your contact details filled in.
4. Open **client-follow-up-tracker.csv**, delete the three example rows, and add your last three finished projects. Most people find at least one client they should have checked in with months ago.

## How to use it on each project (about 2 hours in total, spread over a week)

1. When the client approves the final draft, open **wrap-up-checklist.md** and start at Stage 1.
2. Fill in the handover document while the details are fresh. Send it with email 1 (final delivery).
3. Send the final invoice the same day, using email 2.
4. Three to five working days later, once they have used the work, send email 3 with the questions from **feedback-questions.md**.
5. If the feedback is positive, ask permission to quote them (email 4) and, a few days later, ask for a referral (email 5).
6. Add the project to **client-follow-up-tracker.csv** and set calendar reminders for the 1, 3 and 6 month check-ins (emails 6-8).
7. Within two weeks, write the case study using **case-study-template.md** while you still remember the details.

## Using the tracker

Dates are written as YYYY-MM-DD so the columns sort correctly. Leave a cell empty until that step happens. Once a month, look for rows where **delivered_date** was 1, 3 or 6 months ago but the matching **check_in_1m**, **check_in_3m** or **check_in_6m** cell is still empty: those clients are due a check-in. Also look at **feedback_score** and **repeat_work** together: clients who score 9-10 and get regular check-ins are usually where repeat projects come from.

## Tips that make the biggest difference

- **Invoice on delivery day.** Every day between delivery and invoice is a day the client's attention moves on to something else.
- **Ask for feedback before you ask for anything else.** It gives an unhappy client a private way to tell you, and gives a happy client a moment to remember why they liked working with you.
- **Only quote what clients actually said, with their permission.** Never write a review for them or edit their words beyond fixing a typo they have approved.
- **Make the referral ask specific.** "Do you know one other person who..." works far better than "let me know if you know anyone".
- **Check in with something useful, not "just checking in".** Each check-in email in this kit gives the client a reason to reply.

## Notes

These templates are general business writing, not legal advice. Rules on using client names, logos and quotes in marketing vary by country and by contract, so check your contract and get clear written permission before publishing anything about a client. The example names, figures and companies in this kit are made up for illustration.

This kit pairs well with the Freelance Client Onboarding Kit (the start of a project), the Freelance Proposal Kit (winning the next one) and the Freelancer Get-Paid Kit (chasing late payments).
files.case-study-template.md:
# Case Study Template

A case study is a short story about one project: what the client needed, what you did, and what changed. It is the most persuasive thing you can show a new client, because it proves you have solved a problem like theirs before.

Write it within two weeks of finishing the project, while you remember the details. Aim for 300-500 words. It should take about 45 minutes.

## Before you start

- [ ] You have the client's feedback (see **feedback-questions.md**). Questions 3 and 4 give you the before and after.
- [ ] You know whether you may name the client. If not, describe them instead ("a family-run bakery", "a 20-person software company").
- [ ] You have two or three images or screenshots of the work you are allowed to show.
- [ ] Any numbers you plan to use come from the client or from data you can check. Never estimate or round up a result to make it sound better.

---

## Blank template

### [Headline: the result, in plain words]

*Example headline styles:* "A timetable that updates itself in two minutes" / "From three-week quotes to same-day quotes" / "A brand that finally fits the shop".

**Client:** [Name, or a short description if you can't name them]
**Type of work:** [e.g. website redesign, brand refresh, report writing]
**Timeline:** [e.g. five weeks]

#### The situation

[2-4 sentences. What was going on before you arrived? What was it costing the client in time, money or stress? Use their words from feedback question 3 where you can.]

#### What they needed

[1-3 sentences or a short list. The goal, in the client's terms, not yours.]

#### What I did

[3-6 bullet points. Focus on decisions and why you made them, not a list of software.]

- [Step or decision, and why]
- [Step or decision, and why]
- [Step or decision, and why]

#### The result

[2-4 sentences. What changed? Use the client's answer to feedback question 4. Only include numbers the client gave you or that you can verify.]

#### In their words

> "[An approved quote, exactly as the client agreed it can be used.]"
> [Name, role, company, as approved]

#### Working on something similar?

[One sentence inviting the reader to get in touch, and how.]

---

## Completed example

### A class timetable the studio can update in two minutes

**Client:** Willow Lane Yoga, a two-room yoga studio
**Type of work:** Website redesign
**Timeline:** Four weeks

#### The situation

Willow Lane's old website was built years ago and only the original developer could change it. Class times changed every term, but the website rarely kept up. The owner told me: "Our old site was impossible to change, so the class times were always wrong." Front-desk staff were spending part of every evening answering calls about which classes were on.

#### What they needed

A website the owner could update herself in a few minutes, with a timetable members could trust.

#### What I did

- **Started with the timetable, not the homepage.** It was the page members used most, so I designed it first and built the rest of the site around it.
- **Made one weekly grid the single source of truth.** The studio edits one table and the change shows everywhere the class appears.
- **Wrote a one-page handover guide** with screenshots of the three tasks the owner does every term: adding a class, cancelling a class and changing a teacher.
- **Tested on the front-desk tablet and on members' phones**, because that is where the timetable is actually read.

#### The result

The owner now updates the timetable herself at the start of each term. In her words, there are "no more phone calls asking if the 6pm class is on", and the new evening class filled within its first week of being listed.

#### In their words

> "You explained every step without jargon."
> Priya, owner, Willow Lane Yoga

#### Working on something similar?

If your website is hard to keep up to date, send me a short note about what you need to change most often, and I'll tell you how I would approach it.

*(Willow Lane Yoga and Priya are fictional, created for this example.)*

---

## Where to use it

- Your website portfolio page (one case study per kind of work you want more of).
- Attached to, or linked from, proposals for similar projects.
- A short version (headline, two sentences, quote) in your email signature or on social media.
- Ask yourself after writing it: "Would a client like this one read this and think 'that's my problem too'?" If yes, it is done.

files.closing-emails.md:
# Closing Emails

Eight emails for the end of a project and the months after it. Replace everything in [square brackets]. Keep them short; each one has a single job.

Suggested timing:

| # | Email | When |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Final delivery | The day the final version is approved |
| 2 | Final invoice | Same day as email 1 (or in the same email) |
| 3 | Feedback request | 3-5 working days after delivery |
| 4 | Permission to quote | When positive feedback arrives |
| 5 | Referral ask | 3-7 days after email 4 (or after email 3 if you skip 4) |
| 6 | One-month check-in | About 4 weeks after delivery |
| 7 | Three-month check-in | About 3 months after delivery |
| 8 | Six-month check-in | About 6 months after delivery |

---

## 1. Final delivery

**Subject:** [Project name]: final files and handover

Hi [First name],

Thank you for approving the final version. Everything is now ready for you.

- **Files:** [where they are, e.g. "in the 'Final' folder I've shared with you"]
- **Handover document:** attached. It lists what you received, where everything lives, which accounts are in your name, and how to make common updates yourself.

Please take a look in the next few days and let me know if anything doesn't open or work as expected. Fixes for anything that doesn't match what we agreed are included until [date].

It's been a pleasure working on this with you.

[Your name]

---

## 2. Final invoice

**Subject:** Invoice [number] for [project name]

Hi [First name],

Attached is the final invoice for [project name].

- Project total: [amount]
- Deposit paid: [amount]
- [Agreed extras, if any: amount]
- **Balance due: [amount], by [date]**

You can pay by [payment method and details]. Once it's paid I'll confirm that everything listed in the handover document is yours to use.

Thanks again,
[Your name]

---

## 3. Feedback request

**Subject:** Two minutes of feedback on [project name]?

Hi [First name],

Now that you've had a few days with [the new website / the designs / the report], I'd really value your honest view. It helps me improve, and if anything isn't quite right I'd rather hear it now so I can help.

There are seven short questions below. One-line answers are perfect.

[Paste the seven questions from feedback-questions.md]

Thank you,
[Your name]

---

## 4. Permission to quote

Send this only if the feedback was positive. Quote their own words exactly.

**Subject:** Could I share what you said?

Hi [First name],

Thank you so much for the kind feedback. This part in particular made my day:

> "[Their exact words, copied from their reply]"

Would you be happy for me to show that on my website and in proposals, with your name and company as below?

**[First name Last name], [Role], [Company]**

If you'd prefer just your first name, or no name at all, that's completely fine. Just let me know, and if you'd rather I didn't use it at all, no problem whatsoever.

[Your name]

*Tip: only publish the words they approve, exactly as approved. Save their reply as your record of permission.*

---

## 5. Referral ask

**Subject:** A small favour

Hi [First name],

I'm glad [project name] has worked out well. Most of my work comes from people recommending me, so I wanted to ask:

Do you know **one** other [type of business or person, e.g. "café or food business owner"] who's thinking about [the problem you solve, e.g. "refreshing their website"] this year?

If someone comes to mind, you're welcome to forward this email, or I'm happy for you to share my email address with them. No pressure at all if not.

Thanks either way,
[Your name]

---

## 6. One-month check-in

**Subject:** How is [deliverable] working out?

Hi [First name],

It's been about a month since we wrapped up [project name], so I wanted to check in. Is everything working the way you hoped? Has anything come up that's been confusing or awkward to update?

One thing I've noticed helps clients at this stage: [a practical tip specific to their deliverable, e.g. "updating the Home page special once a week tends to bring more people to the Order page"].

[Your name]

---

## 7. Three-month check-in

**Subject:** An idea for [company]

Hi [First name],

I was thinking about [company] recently and had an idea you might find useful: [one concrete, relevant suggestion, e.g. "a one-page catering menu for office orders, using the same template we built"].

No need to act on it. If it's ever something you'd like help with, I'd be happy to put together a short quote. And if there's anything else on your list for the next few months, I'd love to hear about it.

[Your name]

---

## 8. Six-month check-in

**Subject:** Planning ahead for [season / next quarter]?

Hi [First name],

It's been about six months since we finished [project name]. Many of my clients use this point to plan what's next, for example [two relevant examples, e.g. "a seasonal menu update or a small photo shoot of new products"].

I'm booking projects for [month or quarter] now. If anything is on your mind, reply with a line or two and I'll suggest a few options with prices.

Hope business is going well,
[Your name]

---

## If something goes wrong

If feedback or a check-in reveals a problem, reply within one working day, thank them for telling you, and offer a specific next step:

> Thank you for telling me. I'm sorry [the menu page isn't showing on phones]. I'll look at it today and send you an update by [time/day]. If it's something I got wrong, the fix is on me.

Pause all marketing emails (4, 5, 7 and 8) to that client until the problem is solved and they are happy.
files.feedback-questions.md:
# Client Feedback Questions

Seven questions you can paste into an email, a document or any form tool you already use. They take a client about two minutes. Keep the wording simple and always include question 7: it is the one that surfaces problems before they turn into bad word of mouth.

---

## The questions

1. **On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to recommend me to a friend or colleague?**
2. **What was the main reason for that score?**
3. **What problem did this project solve for you?** (Or: what was going on that made you look for help?)
4. **What difference has it made so far?** Any numbers, time saved or reactions from customers are welcome, but a sentence is fine.
5. **What did you like most about working together?**
6. **What is one thing I could have done better?**
7. **Is there anything that isn't working, or that you're unsure about?**

Optional, for longer projects:

8. How did you find me?
9. Is there anything else you'd like help with in the next six months?

---

## How to read the answers

### The score (question 1)

| Score | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 9-10 | Happy and likely to recommend you | Send email 4 (permission to quote) and email 5 (referral ask). |
| 7-8 | Satisfied but not enthusiastic | Thank them, read question 6 carefully, skip the referral ask for now, keep the check-ins. |
| 0-6 | Something went wrong | Reply personally within one working day. Ask what would make it right. No marketing emails until it is fixed. |

Record the score in **client-follow-up-tracker.csv**. After ten projects, look at your average and at which kinds of projects score lowest.

### The words (questions 2-5)

- Questions 3 and 4 give you the **before and after** for a case study. Copy the client's wording; it is usually clearer than your own.
- Question 5 often contains the best quote. Ask permission before using it (email 4).
- If several clients mention the same thing (for example "fast replies" or "explained things clearly"), put it on your website and in proposals. It is what people actually value about you.

### The criticism (question 6 and 7)

- Thank the client for it, every time. People who tell you what went wrong are doing you a favour.
- Sort each point into one of three boxes:
  - **Fix now:** something in this project that does not work as agreed.
  - **Change my process:** something that would help every future client (for example, clearer timelines, a mid-project check-in).
  - **Note only:** a preference specific to this client.
- Add one "change my process" item to your onboarding or proposal templates each month.

---

## A worked example

A client running a small yoga studio answered:

1. **9**
2. "You made it really simple, and the timetable is finally easy to update."
3. "Our old site was impossible to change, so the class times were always wrong."
4. "No more phone calls asking if the 6pm class is on. Bookings for the new evening class filled in a week."
5. "You explained every step without jargon."
6. "The first draft took a bit longer than I expected."
7. "No, all good."

What the freelancer did next:

- Sent email 4, asking permission to quote the answer to question 5 with the client's first name and studio name. The client agreed.
- Noted "first draft timing" as a **change my process** item and added a line to the proposal template: "You'll see the first draft on [date]."
- Used questions 3 and 4 as the before and after in a case study (see **case-study-template.md**).
- Logged score 9, quote approved: yes, in the tracker.

# Handover Document Template

A handover document is one or two pages the client keeps after the project. It answers the questions they will otherwise email you about in three months: "Where are the files?", "Which font was that?", "How do I update this?". It also makes the end of the project feel finished and professional.

Fill in the blank template below, then read the completed example at the end to see the level of detail to aim for. Delete any section that does not apply to your kind of work.

---

## Blank template

# [Project name]: Handover

**Prepared for:** [Client name, company]
**Prepared by:** [Your name, business name]
**Date:** [Date]
**Project period:** [Start date] to [End date]

### 1. What you received

| Item | Format | Where it is |
|---|---|---|
| [Deliverable 1] | [e.g. PDF, PNG, source file] | [Folder name or link name] |
| [Deliverable 2] | | |
| [Deliverable 3] | | |

### 2. Where everything lives

- **Main folder:** [Name of shared folder or download, and who owns it]
- **Source / editable files:** [Location]
- **Final exports:** [Location]
- **Anything else (accounts, licences, hosting):** [Location and whose account it is in]

### 3. Accounts, licences and logins

| What | Account owner | Renewal date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [e.g. font licence, stock images, plugin, domain] | [Client's email] | [Date or "one-off"] | [e.g. covers web and print use] |

Passwords are never written in this document. [Explain how they were transferred, e.g. "sent separately via your password manager" or "reset to your email address".]

### 4. How to use it

[Three to six short, practical instructions. For example: how to update a price on the website, which logo file to use on dark backgrounds, how to export a new page from the template.]

1. [Instruction]
2. [Instruction]
3. [Instruction]

### 5. What to avoid

- [e.g. Do not stretch the logo; resize it from a corner.]
- [e.g. Do not edit the master template; make a copy first.]

### 6. What was out of scope

[List anything discussed but not included, so nobody assumes it was done. For example: "Translations into other languages", "Social media templates", "Ongoing updates after launch".]

### 7. Support after handover

- [e.g. "Fixes for anything that does not work as agreed are included until [date]."]
- [e.g. "New changes or additions are billed at [rate] or quoted as a new project."]
- **Best way to reach me:** [Email]. I usually reply within [time].

### 8. Ownership and usage

[One or two sentences matching your contract. For example: "On receipt of full payment, you own the final designs listed in section 1. Third-party items (fonts, stock images) are licensed, not owned, under the terms listed in section 3."]

---

## Completed example

# Harbour Street Bakery website refresh: Handover

**Prepared for:** Dana Okafor, Harbour Street Bakery
**Prepared by:** Sam Ríos, Ríos Studio
**Date:** 14 March
**Project period:** 6 February to 14 March

### 1. What you received

| Item | Format | Where it is |
|---|---|---|
| Five-page website (Home, Menu, Order, About, Contact) | Live site plus theme files | Your website account; theme backup in "03 Website" folder |
| Logo refresh: full logo, icon, wordmark | SVG, PNG (light and dark), PDF | "01 Logo" folder |
| Menu board template | Editable presentation file plus print PDF | "02 Print" folder |
| Brand sheet (colours, fonts, spacing) | PDF, one page | "01 Logo" folder |

### 2. Where everything lives

- **Main folder:** "Harbour Street - Final" in your own shared drive. You own it; I have edit access until 28 March.
- **Source / editable files:** "01 Logo/source" and "02 Print/source"
- **Final exports:** each folder's "export" subfolder
- **Website:** your website builder account, registered to orders@ (your email)

### 3. Accounts, licences and logins

| What | Account owner | Renewal date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Website builder plan | Your business email | Yearly, 2 February | Basic plan is enough for current traffic |
| Domain name | Your business email | Yearly, 19 May | Auto-renew is switched on |
| Heading font licence | Your business email | One-off | Covers web, print and signage |
| Four stock photos (Order page) | Your business email | One-off | Standard licence, no resale on merchandise |

Passwords are not in this document. Your website login was reset to your email address on 13 March, and I no longer have the password.

### 4. How to use it

1. **Change a menu price:** log in, open the Menu page, click the price, type the new one, press Publish. It is live in about a minute.
2. **Add a seasonal special:** duplicate the "Special" block on the Home page, change the text and photo, publish. Delete it when the season ends.
3. **Make a new menu board:** open the template in "02 Print/source", choose File > Make a copy, edit the copy, export as PDF at A3 size for the shop printer.
4. **Logo on dark backgrounds:** use the files ending in `-light.png`. On light backgrounds use `-dark.png`.

### 5. What to avoid

- Do not upload photos larger than 2 MB; the site will slow down on phones. Resize to 2000 pixels wide first.
- Do not change the heading font in the website settings; the licence only covers the one we chose.

### 6. What was out of scope

- Online payments on the Order page (orders currently arrive by email, as agreed).
- Social media templates.
- Photography of new products.

### 7. Support after handover

- Fixes for anything that does not work as agreed are included until 14 April.
- New pages or features are quoted as a separate project; small edits are billed in 30-minute blocks at my current rate.
- **Best way to reach me:** the studio email address on my invoices. I usually reply within one working day.

### 8. Ownership and usage

Your final invoice was paid on 14 March, so you now own the logo, website design and menu template listed in section 1. The font and stock photos are licensed to you under the terms in section 3.
files.wrap-up-checklist.md:
# Project Wrap-Up Checklist

Copy this list for each project. Tick each line as you go. Most projects take about two hours of work in total, spread across a week or two.

Project: ____________________   Client: ____________________

Final approval date: __________   Final invoice sent: __________   Paid: __________

---

## Stage 1: Before you call it finished (day 0)

- [ ] The client has approved the final version **in writing** (an email or message is enough). Save it in the project folder.
- [ ] Compare what you delivered against the original scope or proposal. Every promised item is either delivered or has a written note explaining why not.
- [ ] Any extra work done outside the scope is listed, with its agreed price, so it can go on the final invoice.
- [ ] Open change requests are closed: done, declined, or quoted as a separate project.
- [ ] You have checked the deliverables one last time on a clean device or account (links work, files open, fonts are included, nothing points to your own drafts).

## Stage 2: Deliver and hand over (day 0-1)

- [ ] Final files are exported in the formats agreed in the scope (for example print PDF plus web PNG, or source files plus build).
- [ ] Files are named clearly: `client-project-item-v-final.ext`, not `final_FINAL_2.ext`.
- [ ] Files are uploaded to one shared location the client controls, or delivered as one download. Avoid sending files across several emails.
- [ ] Any accounts, logins or licences bought for the client are transferred to the client's own email address. You do not keep the only copy of anything they own.
- [ ] Your own access to the client's systems is listed so it can be removed (see Stage 5).
- [ ] The handover document is filled in (use **handover-document-template.md**).
- [ ] Email 1 (final delivery) is sent with the handover document attached.

## Stage 3: Get paid (day 0-1, then follow up)

- [ ] Final invoice is sent the same day as delivery, using email 2.
- [ ] The invoice lists: deposit already paid, remaining balance, any agreed extras, due date and how to pay.
- [ ] The due date is in your calendar. If it passes, follow your usual reminder sequence.
- [ ] Payment received and recorded in your books.
- [ ] If your contract says ownership or licence of the work passes on full payment, confirm that in writing once paid ("Payment received, thank you. Everything listed in the handover document is now yours to use.").

## Stage 4: Learn and build reputation (day 3-14)

- [ ] Day 3-5: Email 3 (feedback request) sent with the questions from **feedback-questions.md**.
- [ ] Feedback received and read. Any problem raised gets a personal reply within one working day.
- [ ] If the feedback was positive: email 4 (permission to quote) sent. Their exact approved words saved in the tracker.
- [ ] A few days after that: email 5 (referral ask) sent.
- [ ] Case study drafted with **case-study-template.md**. Client approval obtained before publishing anything that names them.
- [ ] Portfolio or website updated.

## Stage 5: Close the project (day 7-14)

- [ ] Your access to client systems removed, or the client asked to remove it. Note the date.
- [ ] Project folder tidied: final files, approval email, contract, invoices, handover document. Drafts archived or deleted as your contract requires.
- [ ] Hours and costs compared with the quote. Write one line: "Quoted __ hours, used __ hours. Next time I will ___."
- [ ] Project added to **client-follow-up-tracker.csv** with dates for the 1, 3 and 6 month check-ins.
- [ ] Calendar reminders set for each check-in.

## Stage 6: Stay in touch (months 1, 3 and 6)

- [ ] Month 1: email 6 sent (how is it working?).
- [ ] Month 3: email 7 sent (something useful, plus a light offer).
- [ ] Month 6: email 8 sent (planning ahead).
- [ ] Tracker updated each time with the date and any reply.

---

## Five mistakes this checklist prevents

1. **Delivering before written approval.** Without it, "one more small change" can go on for weeks.
2. **Invoicing a week later.** Payment usually takes longer the later the invoice arrives.
3. **Keeping the client's assets hostage by accident.** A domain, font licence or stock photo bought on your account becomes a problem the day you are on holiday.
4. **Asking for a referral from a client who is quietly unhappy.** Feedback first, always.
5. **Never speaking to the client again.** Past clients who already trust you are usually the cheapest source of new work you have.
